item.text: {"piece_id":"02","title":"A CAD File Is Not Yet an Engineering Workflow","question":"Which claims withstand scrutiny, and where are the evidence or interpretations in tension?","argument":"The strongest current evidence supports narrow, end-to-end CAD conversions with explicit artifact checks—not autonomous engineering workflows. Engineering.com found that Backflip outputs matched mass on two controlled drawing-to-CAD tasks after STEP export, yet its native Fusion import was incomplete and it failed a multibody case; meanwhile, robot-agent results show that broad task scores can conceal sharply different failure modes. For engineering leaders, the issue is not whether a model can produce an apparently valid result, but whether the deployed toolchain preserves the properties their downstream workflow needs.","synthesis":"The Backflip tests and the MIT-CDFG survey together identify portability as a missing evaluation layer between generated geometry and usable engineering output. A mass match after importing a neutral STEP file establishes that a particular solid has the target volume under a chosen material, while incomplete feature-tree import shows that editability and design intent may not survive the same workflow. The robotics evidence sharpens the operational implication: aggregate success counts also hide task-specific gaps, so CAD evaluations should separately test geometry, native editability, tolerance compliance, manufacturability, and downstream execution rather than treat one score as a proxy for all of them.","limitations":"The Backflip evidence consists of three TooTallToby exercises and informal photo/video trials, not production drawings with tolerance stacks, assemblies, or fabrication outcomes. The Physical AI Podcast transcript is automatic and its numerical account should be checked against the underlying study before publication; NVIDIA’s simulation description is a company executive’s
